title: What do we build with the limits?
premise: The last sequence turns the museum back towards its makers. Each hall exposes a different decision: what can be distinguished, who can participate, what survives disagreement, where a claim comes from, how contributions accumulate, which connections form, which bodies a catalogue permits, and what we will change next.

halls.title: Distinguish
halls.question: How much space does a distinction need?
halls.inherit: Transformation gave us interpolation; arrays gave each word an address. Those operations now distribute room between labels.
halls.action: Choose two pink labels. Move the Perspective slider partway, compare their separation, then repeat with two grey labels. Hold the slider at one value while moving your own viewpoint.
halls.observation: The slider changes the positions of the labels themselves. Moving your head changes the view of that arrangement. Keep these two transformations separate.
halls.explanation: The index i keeps a word attached to its two authored positions. lerp blends those positions; blend chooses how far the word has travelled. The same operation learned in transformation can make a distinction easier or harder to see. The script calls this perspective, but it changes the represented geometry. It is not a camera command.
halls.critical: The two groups and both arrangements were chosen by the maker. This is a spatial argument about compression, not a measurement of a trained language model. Its pink category can itself flatten the people it asks us to distinguish. Name one difference within that category that matters to you. The queer opening is a demand to revise the representation, not a promise that expanding every distance will produce justice.
halls.next_test: Compare a named pair at three slider positions from the same viewing distance, then ask whether the labels remain distinguishable from the intended approach. Record the pair and viewpoint before generalising this to other dense displays.
halls.carry: A representation allocates distinctions. A room allocates opportunities to address one another.
halls.technical: The seeded position generator uses seed 42 and two arrays of twelve terms. A horizontal slider calls _on_perspective_changed(), clamps its input and updates MultiMesh instance transforms and label positions. The map places the default blend; perspective_blend is also configurable for authors. The exhibit does not train, query or evaluate an embedding model. Inspect the expanding grey group's clearance at both endpoints; its configured offset and spread exceed the initial compact cloud.

halls.title: Arrange
halls.question: Who becomes easy to address before anyone speaks?
halls.inherit: The previous hall moved labels. Here positions, count and scale arrange possible participants.
halls.action: Walk around the paired miniature rooms. Count every chair in each. Compare the head chair with a side chair, then compare two chairs around the round table. Imagine a participant who needs a clear sightline to an interpreter.
halls.observation: The long-table model has a head chair and six smaller side chairs. The circle has six equally scaled chairs. Count, scale, colour and position change together; the pair is not an experiment that isolates table shape.
halls.explanation: Six iterations divide a full turn, TAU, into equal angles. cos and sin place each chair on a ring around origin. The little circle carries the arrays, transformations and waves we have already learned. Equal spacing is what this loop guarantees. Equal opportunity to speak would require another kind of evidence.
halls.critical: The green circle arrives already recommended by its colour. Before accepting that judgement, consider sightlines, hearing, turning and entry. A shared centre can be useful without meeting every body's needs. Geometry sets conditions for participation; it does not contain the participants' agreements or resolve unequal authority. The next design should let those conditions be compared with people using the space.
halls.next_test: Build a comparison with equal chair count, scale and colour, changing only the arrangement. Test sightlines and approach routes before claiming the circle is more accessible. Keep the present pair as the openly persuasive first example.
halls.carry: A place at the table does not make every account agree. The next hall keeps two accounts visible.
halls.technical: The placed default is plan=pair. _build_centralized_room() creates a separate head chair plus a nested 3-by-2 loop of chairs at scale 0.6*s. _build_distributed_room() creates six chairs at scale s. Other implemented author configurations are head, circle, panopticon and vacant. They are map/editor parameters, not visitor buttons in this placement. This primary exhibit is a passive miniature; it runs no classifier or turn-taking simulation.

halls.title: Keep the conflict
halls.question: What disappears when a disagreement is declared resolved?
halls.inherit: Different positions can produce different requirements. Preserving the requirements is the first step towards inspecting their conflict.
halls.action: Read branch A and branch B and locate the light between them. Give each branch a concrete report about one door, including a time and a source. Decide whether your reports actually contradict each other before proposing a resolution.
halls.observation: The placed junction keeps two upright pillars and a pulsing marker. It displays a relation; it does not run a merge algorithm or derive logical consequences.
halls.explanation: There is a second arrangement in the source that this placement does not show. In resolved, A keeps its full height and B becomes a labelled stump. The two builder calls make resolution visible as a change in what remains. That is an authored picture of a decision, not a proof that the decision was warranted.
halls.critical: Two stored reports need not be a contradiction: they might concern different doors or different times. Preserving sources helps investigate that difference. It does not by itself change the rules of inference. The paraconsistent question is narrower: when both P and not-P are admitted, can unrelated conclusions still be refused? The sculpture makes room for that question but cannot answer it through overlapping meshes. Its unresolved glow should invite investigation rather than make conflict desirable in every case.
halls.next_test: Add a small inspectable inference table with a contradictory pair and an unrelated proposition. Require the visitor to predict which consequences follow. Compare that with preserving two source-tagged reports, so storage and inference remain distinct lessons.
halls.carry: To investigate disagreement we need to know where each claim came from.
halls.technical: merge defaults to junction. _build_all() dispatches among junction, overlap, resolved and fork; _process() modulates the marker's emission using sine. The variants are accepted by apply_grid_config(), but the current placement has no live variant selector. The excerpt describes an available author variant, not an action the visitor can take. Keep the Florensky and other supporting exhibits as comparisons; their presence is not evidence that this primary runs a logic engine.

halls.title: Locate the claim
halls.question: Which part of a judgement tells you where it came from?
halls.inherit: The conflict room asked for sources. Here the source travels visibly with the verdict.
halls.action: Read all four panels. Keep SUBJECT #4729 fixed in your comparison and record each verdict, confidence and footer. Return to the first panel and identify which fields changed between panels.
halls.observation: Four authored verdicts share one identifier. Your movement changes which panel you read. It does not make a panel recalculate an assessment of you.
halls.explanation: The dictionary supplies a verdict and a confidence; the footer supplies a location. There is a revealing extra decision: this hall explicitly assigns NW, NE, SW and SE through its map tokens. That override takes precedence over the position-based fallback. The four-way disagreement has been composed for us. The percentages have not been earned by measuring the subject.
halls.critical: A visible address makes a claim easier to question, but cannot make it correct. ORDERLY and CREATIVE are not logical negations; they could both describe someone under different criteria. DANGEROUS demands an account of danger to whom and in what circumstances. Even an agreeable label needs evidence. The room's productive limit is the gap between displaying a standpoint and exposing the method that produced its judgement.
halls.next_test: Give each panel an inspectable criterion and the evidence used. Compare disagreement caused by different criteria with disagreement caused by different observations. First verify that all four small panels can be read without losing their footers.
halls.carry: Keeping viewpoints visible is different from combining their contributions into a common object.
halls.technical: There are four placements of the same primary token with #verdict:NW, NE, SW and SE. _resolve_quadrant_key() returns a valid explicit override first; only unconfigured instances use a position hash. The default address=footnote shows provenance on the panel. There is no classifier, player sensor or probability calibration behind QUADRANT_VERDICTS. These placements had been absent from the museum declaration even though they existed in the sequence and grid map.

halls.title: Contribute
halls.question: Does more activity mean more voices?
halls.inherit: The situated panels preserved separate views. This machine sends contributions from a rim into one shared form.
halls.action: Follow a packet from a rim node to the central form. Look for a second contribution from a source you have already seen. Watch a full version fill and restart; compare the new form with the counters that remain.
halls.observation: A returning source can add another facet without adding a new distinct source within that version. On reset the seen-peer flags clear, but the contributor counter persists. Across versions that number counts repeated participation, not unique people.
halls.explanation: Every accepted facet increments the edit count. The Boolean array _seen_peers lets the same source count only once within a version. On the next version those flags clear while the totals persist. A number labelled CONTRIBUTORS can therefore outgrow the twelve source positions. The code tells us what was counted more precisely than the label does.
halls.critical: The shape accepts every arriving contribution. No peer can challenge another's content, and no correction replaces an earlier facet. A growing form is a useful image of collective activity, but its smoothness conceals the work of maintaining knowledge. The counter exposes another loss: attendance across versions is not the same as a growing community. A commons needs ways to preserve disagreement, trace a revision and distinguish repair from accumulation.
halls.next_test: Separate lifetime edits, distinct sources in this version, and lifetime distinct sources in the readout. Check two complete cycles with a repeated source. Then add one disputed contribution whose revision changes an existing facet rather than increasing the pile.
halls.carry: Many sources can still feed a single centre. The next machine changes the rule of connection.
halls.technical: Twelve generated peer positions send packets by default every 0.16 seconds. Each packet's life advances by delta*4; arrival calls _place_facet(). Sixty facets fill the display. Facet positions follow a prescribed helix, not negotiated knowledge. _reset_artifact() clears the form and _seen_peers but does not zero _edits or _contributors. The current contributor label counts source-version participation over time. This is recorded as a next improvement, not silently treated as a count of unique people.

halls.title: Connect
halls.question: Can a network grow without naming a root?
halls.inherit: The commons machine had many sources and one centre. Here a new node chooses several existing neighbours.
halls.action: Watch a new shoot and trace its links. Compare a crowded region with a sparse one. Predict which nearby nodes the next shoot could reach, then inspect what actually appears.
halls.observation: New nodes connect by distance. They have no designated root, but some nodes accumulate more links than others. The little graph sways as a whole; that motion is separate from the creation of edges.
halls.explanation: The neighbour search runs before the new node is inserted, so the shoot cannot select itself. It can only select nodes already present. Up to three nearest neighbours receive a link. The rule creates a graph without declaring a family tree; it also gives earlier and nearby nodes opportunities that later or distant nodes do not have.
halls.critical: No named root is a construction rule, not a certificate of equal power. Proximity and arrival time still shape access. A graph can contain uneven degrees, bottlenecks and dependencies without storing a hierarchy field. The desire for other relations becomes useful when we can ask which relation to change and observe the consequences. Adding a distant link or removing a busy node would make a sharper experiment than simply calling the whole network free.
halls.next_test: Expose a selectable node and removal operation, then show connected components before and after deletion. Compare nearest-only growth with one distant connection per shoot. The current exhibit has neither deletion nor automatic repair.
halls.carry: The assembly laboratory replaces nearest-neighbour growth with a catalogue and an authored target.
halls.technical: The default has max_nodes=40, links_per_node=3, grow_period=0.4 and spread=0.36. Two initial nodes seed the display. _nearest_indices() sorts Euclidean distances; _grow_shoot() inserts a node and its edges. Capacity triggers a fresh small graph. Growth is bounded in a shallow volume. rhizome_cave_demo remains a secondary spatial exhibit; a rootless graph does not prove that the visitor can traverse every part of the room.

halls.title: Assemble a body
halls.question: Where was this body's destination decided?
halls.inherit: We carry primitives, arrays, transformations and restoring forces into a catalogue of possible assemblies.
halls.action: Choose a visible part during the floating phase. Follow it as an assembly forms. Watch another floating phase and a different assembly; notice both its destination and any change of shape or colour.
halls.observation: The controller reuses part instances, but can replace their mesh, type and colour when assigning a new assembly. The same instance need not keep the same visual identity. Target positions are authored before the parts move.
halls.explanation: Here the restoring force returns from the earlier halls. The vector to_target points from a part to its assigned destination. The spring changes velocity and velocity changes position. A moving piece can look as if it has found its place, although another file already supplied the target. dock_damp is applied each frame, which also makes the settling depend on the update rate. The clock remains inside the body we are watching.
halls.critical: The name MolecularDesigner suggests chemistry, but the current controller arranges catalogue parts and draws declared bonds. It does not establish chemical validity. Its constructive question is still substantial: can a new body be made by changing positions and relations, or does it demand a part the inventory cannot supply? Reusing an instance while replacing its visible form offers another question about identity. Neither physical emergence nor freedom is established by a persuasive animation.
halls.next_test: Expose one editable target with a visible link to its source assembly. Compare the same docking motion at two fixed update rates before changing damping. Let a visitor alter one relation and keep the resulting body beside the original.
halls.carry: A useful catalogue is a choice with consequences. The last hall asks us to keep one consequence available for revision.
halls.technical: MolecularDesigner.tscn enables automatic ten-second floating and assembling phases and starts with forty part instances. _assemble() reads node specifications, reapplies each part's catalogue mesh and calls set_target(target_pos); the call does not supply a target basis. Bonds are read from the assembly data. Part._dock_to_target() integrates a damped spring in _process(), while idle translation accumulates a sine-derived offset each frame. Keyboard shortcuts exist in the script, but the book does not rely on them in VR. No in-room catalogue editor or chemistry solver is implemented by this primary.

halls.title: Return with a change
halls.question: Which consequence will you keep in view after the next line arrives?
halls.inherit: Every hall made a choice inspectable. Here we turn that practice towards the museum itself.
halls.action: Read one choice/exclusion pair and keep it in mind after it scrolls away. Choose a room you have walked and name one obstacle, one possible change and one observation that would tell you whether it helped.
halls.observation: The entry count increases while old entries leave the six-line buffer. The examples are prewritten. The display records no visitor decisions and does not save the discussion.
halls.explanation: A line enters at the front; another leaves when the buffer is full. The counter survives that loss. We met a running count near the point at the beginning of the museum. Here counting and remembering separate in four lines of code. The machine can announce progress while the evidence of an earlier problem has already disappeared.
halls.critical: Naming an exclusion does not repair it. Nor should every design limitation be treated as the same kind of harm. Keep the specific body, activity and consequence in view. The next iteration needs a durable record of a change and its outcome, including an outcome we did not expect. Generalisation begins when another hall presents the same relation; it remains a proposal until someone can test that second encounter.
halls.next_test: Make the ledger accept a real museum observation with hall, affected activity, proposed change and later result. Preserve unresolved entries across visits. Begin with the contributor-counter ambiguity or a control whose reach has actually been tested.
halls.carry: Return to one earlier hall. The spine has supplied tools for another pass, not a final inventory of possible bodies.
halls.technical: The defaults are log_interval=1.8 and visible_lines=6. _push_entry() chooses one shared index into the prewritten CHOICES and EXCLUDED arrays, pushes the pair to a bounded buffer and increments _count. The display starts with two entries. _process() advances the timer and animates the lamp and spool. There is no persistent log, visitor input or completion evaluation. The formula and earlier artifacts remain supporting reminders; their presence does not certify the ledger's examples.
